overview: UNION ALL is a SQL set operator that concatenates the result sets of two or more SELECT statements into a single result set, keeping ALL rows including duplicates.
Unlike UNION (without ALL), it does NOT perform a deduplication step, so it skips the expensive distinct sort/hash and is significantly faster.
It requires every participating query to return the same number of columns with compatible data types, in the same positional order.
learningObjectives: Understand how UNION ALL concatenates result sets and why it preserves duplicates.
Learn the performance difference between UNION ALL and UNION and when each is appropriate.
Apply UNION ALL to real pipeline patterns such as merging partitions, shards, and incremental loads.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: UNION ALL is a multiset (bag) union operator that returns the concatenation of the rows produced by two or more compatible SELECT queries, with no elimination of duplicate rows. The result column names and types are derived from the first query, and each subsequent query must be union-compatible (same column count and implicitly castable types).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine you have two stacks of receipts from two cash registers and you want one big pile. UNION ALL just dumps both stacks together into one pile without checking whether any receipt appears twice. It is fast because it never stops to compare and throw away copies.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Set operators (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT) were standardized in SQL-86 and refined through SQL-92 as part of the relational model's set-theoretic foundations championed by Edgar F. Codd. UNION ALL was added because the default UNION's implicit DISTINCT was costly, and practitioners needed a bag-semantics variant for performance and for cases where duplicate rows are meaningful.

whyItMatters.business: Enables fast consolidation of data split across regions, time periods, or systems for unified reporting and dashboards, without silently dropping legitimately repeated records such as identical transactions.
whyItMatters.engineering: Provides a cheap, predictable way to stitch together partitioned or sharded query outputs and to combine incremental deltas with historical data in ELT/ETL pipelines.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because it avoids the sort/hash needed for deduplication, UNION ALL scales far better on large result sets and is the standard primitive for merging many partition scans in parallel query engines.
whyItMatters.cost: Avoiding the deduplication step reduces CPU, memory, and spill-to-disk usage, lowering compute cost in pay-per-query warehouses like BigQuery, Snowflake, and Redshift.
whyItMatters.reliability: Its behavior is deterministic in row count (sum of inputs) and never loses rows, making pipeline outputs auditable and reconcilable against source counts.

coreComponents.name: Branch SELECT Queries
coreComponents.definition: The individual SELECT statements whose outputs are combined.
coreComponents.purpose: Each branch produces a result set that becomes part of the concatenated output.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must return the same number of columns with positionally compatible data types.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT id, amount FROM sales_2023 and SELECT id, amount FROM sales_2024

coreComponents.name: UNION ALL Operator
coreComponents.definition: The keyword pair that concatenates branch outputs without deduplication.
coreComponents.purpose: To append all rows from every branch into one result set, preserving duplicates.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Performs no sort, no hash, and no distinct comparison; simply streams rows from each branch.

coreComponents.name: Output Schema (from first branch)
coreComponents.definition: The column names and inferred result types that label the combined output.
coreComponents.purpose: Defines the structure and aliases of the final result set.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Column names come from the first SELECT; types are the common supertype of each positional column across branches.
coreComponents.examples: Aliases like AS region apply only in the first SELECT to name output columns

internalWorking: The optimizer plans each branch SELECT independently, often as separate scans or subplans that can run in parallel.
The execution engine appends (concatenates) the rows from each branch into the output stream as they are produced; no buffering for comparison is required.
Because there is no DISTINCT step, the planner adds no sort or hash-aggregate node above the union, unlike plain UNION which inserts a deduplication operator.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Branch 1 (SELECT) + Branch 2 (SELECT) + ... -> Concatenate rows (no dedup) -> Combined Result Set
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. The engine reads rows from the first SELECT branch and emits them directly to the output.
2. It then reads rows from the second SELECT branch and appends them, again with no comparison.
3. Duplicate rows from either branch are retained; the total row count equals the sum of the branch row counts.
4. The combined stream is returned (or fed to an ORDER BY / outer query) using the column names from the first branch.

keyTerminology.meaning: A collection that allows duplicate elements, as opposed to a mathematical set.
keyTerminology.importance: UNION ALL uses bag semantics, which is exactly why it keeps duplicates and is cheaper than set-based UNION.

keyTerminology.meaning: The requirement that all branches return the same number of columns with implicitly convertible data types in the same order.
keyTerminology.importance: Violating it causes a compile-time error; matching is positional, not by column name.

keyTerminology.meaning: The process of removing duplicate rows, performed by UNION via an implicit DISTINCT.
keyTerminology.importance: UNION ALL explicitly skips this step, which is the source of its performance advantage.

importantConcepts.explanation: Branches are combined by column position, not name. The first column of every branch lines up regardless of alias, so ordering and types must be aligned deliberately.
When branch columns differ in type (e.g., INT and DECIMAL), the engine promotes each positional column to a common supertype. Incompatible types (e.g., date vs. text in some dialects) raise an error.

importantConcepts.concept: ORDER BY Applies to the Whole Result
importantConcepts.explanation: An ORDER BY clause is only valid at the end and sorts the entire concatenated result, not individual branches. To sort within a branch you must wrap it or use a tagging column.

variationsAndTypes: **UNION ALL (bag union):** Concatenates and keeps all duplicates; the fastest set operator.
**UNION (set union):** Concatenates then removes duplicate rows via an implicit DISTINCT, requiring a sort or hash.
**Multi-branch UNION ALL:** Chaining many SELECTs (common when merging dozens of monthly partitions) into one result set.
advantages: **Performance:** No deduplication means no sort/hash, so it is dramatically faster on large inputs.
**Predictable Row Count:** Output rows equal the sum of input rows, simplifying reconciliation and auditing.
**Lower Resource Use:** Avoids memory pressure and disk spills caused by distinct operations.
**Streaming Friendly:** Branches can be pipelined and parallelized, ideal for partition and shard merges.
disadvantages: **Retains Unwanted Duplicates:** If branches legitimately overlap, duplicates appear in the output and can skew counts or sums.
**No Implicit Cleansing:** Unlike UNION, it will not silently fix overlapping data, shifting responsibility to the developer.
**Positional Fragility:** Mismatched column order across branches compiles silently if types happen to align, producing wrong results.
**Type Coercion Surprises:** Implicit type promotion can change precision or formatting unexpectedly.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use UNION ALL when branches are known to be disjoint (e.g., separate partitions, shards, or time windows), when duplicates are meaningful, or when performance matters and you do not need deduplication.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid UNION ALL when you specifically need a distinct set of rows and the branches may overlap; in that case use UNION (or add explicit DISTINCT logic) so duplicates are removed correctly.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: UNION ALL is like merging two guest lists into one master list by simply taping them together. You get every name from both lists, even if the same person was invited by two different hosts. UNION, by contrast, would cross out the repeated names so each guest appears once.

commonMisconceptions.myth: UNION and UNION ALL produce the same result, just one is faster.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ semantically: UNION removes duplicate rows while UNION ALL keeps them. They only produce identical output when the branches contain no overlapping or internally duplicated rows.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Columns are matched by name, so order does not matter.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Set operators match columns by position. If you list columns in a different order in one branch, values will be merged into the wrong output columns even though the query compiles.

productionConsiderations.scalability: UNION ALL is the preferred primitive for merging many partition or shard scans because branches parallelize and no global deduplication barrier is needed; it scales near-linearly with input size.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Deterministic row counts make it easy to reconcile combined output against the sum of source counts, catching missing or extra branches early.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because branches are independent, partial failures are easier to isolate; a failing branch can be re-run without affecting others in a recomputed pipeline.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track per-branch row counts and total output count; a divergence between expected sum and actual output signals a branch error or an accidental UNION.
productionConsiderations.security: Each branch is subject to its own table-level access controls; combining them does not bypass row or column security on the underlying sources.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Replacing UNION with UNION ALL where duplicates are impossible removes sort/hash compute, often cutting query cost meaningfully in warehouse engines.
productionConsiderations.performance: Avoid wrapping UNION ALL in unnecessary outer DISTINCT or ORDER BY when not needed, as that reintroduces the deduplication/sort cost you were avoiding.

codeExamples.title: Merging Yearly Partition Tables with UNION ALL
codeExamples.overview: Combine sales from two separate yearly tables into one result set, keeping every row because the partitions are disjoint by year.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM sales_2023
UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount
FROM sales_2024;
codeExamples.breakdown: Both branches return four positionally aligned columns of compatible types. Because the two tables hold non-overlapping years, no duplicates exist, making UNION ALL both correct and faster than UNION.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A single result set containing every row from sales_2023 followed by every row from sales_2024; total rows equal the sum of both table counts.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Listing columns in a different order in one branch silently mixes values into the wrong columns. Mismatched column counts raise a compile error.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Since the partitions cannot overlap, never use plain UNION here; it would add an unnecessary deduplication sort over the entire combined set.

codeExamples.title: Tagging Branch Source and Demonstrating Duplicate Retention
codeExamples.overview: Add a literal source-tag column to each branch and show how UNION ALL keeps an identical row that appears in both inputs.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT 'web' AS channel, customer_id, amount
FROM web_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT 'store' AS channel, customer_id, amount
FROM store_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT 'web' AS channel, customer_id, amount
FROM web_orders_backfill
ORDER BY channel, customer_id;
codeExamples.breakdown: A constant literal labels each branch's origin. The third branch may repeat rows already present in the first; UNION ALL keeps them. The single ORDER BY at the end sorts the entire combined result.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: All rows from the three branches concatenated, with a channel column showing origin, sorted by channel then customer_id. Identical rows from web_orders and web_orders_backfill both appear.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Placing ORDER BY inside a branch is invalid; it must appear only after the final SELECT. Aliases set in later branches are ignored for output naming.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you must remove cross-branch duplicates introduced by a backfill, wrap the UNION ALL in a SELECT DISTINCT or use UNION only on the overlapping branches, not the whole set.

codeExamples.title: UNION ALL vs UNION Showing Row Count Difference
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrate that UNION removes duplicates while UNION ALL keeps them using overlapping literal rows.
codeExamples.code:
-- Returns 4 rows (duplicates kept)
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'A'),(2,'B')) AS t(id, val)
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,'B'),(3,'C')) AS s(id, val);

-- Returns 3 rows (duplicate (2,''B'') removed)
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'A'),(2,'B')) AS t(id, val)
UNION
SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,'B'),(3,'C')) AS s(id, val);
codeExamples.breakdown: The two inputs share the row (2,'B'). UNION ALL emits it twice (4 rows total), whereas UNION deduplicates and emits it once (3 rows total), at the cost of a sort/hash step.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: First query returns 4 rows including two copies of (2,'B'); second query returns 3 distinct rows.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming both forms return the same count. NULLs are treated as equal to each other during UNION deduplication, which can surprise developers.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Reach for UNION ALL by default and only escalate to UNION when you have confirmed duplicates must be eliminated.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer stores transactions in monthly partition tables and also receives a nightly incremental delta file. Analysts need one unified, fast query that reports total revenue across all months plus the latest delta, without the cost of deduplicating millions of rows that are already known to be unique by transaction id.
endToEndExample.inputData: Twelve monthly tables sales_2024_01 ... sales_2024_12, each with (txn_id, store_id, txn_ts, amount), plus a staging table sales_delta with the same schema holding today's new transactions.
endToEndExample.architecture: A columnar data warehouse (e.g., Snowflake or BigQuery) holding the monthly partition tables and the delta staging table. A reporting view combines them with UNION ALL and is queried by a BI dashboard.
processingSteps: 1. Confirm each partition and the delta are disjoint by txn_id so no real duplicates exist.
2. Write a view that UNION ALLs all twelve monthly SELECTs plus the delta SELECT, with identical column lists in the same order.
3. Add a literal source-month tag column to each branch for traceability.
4. Expose the view to the BI tool; aggregate revenue with SUM(amount) over the combined result.
5. Reconcile the view's row count against the sum of source table counts as a data-quality gate.
endToEndExample.output: A single logical relation containing all transactions for the year plus the latest delta, with total row count equal to the sum of all source counts, ready for fast aggregation.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Compare COUNT(*) of the view to the summed COUNT(*) of all source tables in a scheduled check; alert if they diverge, which would indicate a missing branch or accidental deduplication.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a branch's schema drifts (e.g., a renamed column), the view fails to compile, surfacing the error immediately. A type mismatch on amount across branches is caught at view-definition time.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Analysts get sub-second aggregate revenue across the full year and the delta, at substantially lower compute cost than a UNION-based equivalent, with auditable row counts for trust.

industryUseCases.company: Data Warehousing Teams (e.g., Snowflake, BigQuery users)
industryUseCases.problem: Querying across many monthly or daily partition tables that together represent one logical dataset.
industryUseCases.solution: Define a view or query that UNION ALLs each partition SELECT, relying on the fact that partitions are disjoint to skip deduplication.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast, low-cost unified access to historical data without the sort/hash overhead of UNION, with predictable row counts.

industryUseCases.problem: Aggregating reporting data spread across multiple database shards keyed by tenant or region.
industryUseCases.solution: Run the same SELECT against each shard and UNION ALL the per-shard results in a federation layer, since shards hold non-overlapping keys.
industryUseCases.benefits: Linear scaling across shards and correct totals without expensive cross-shard deduplication.

industryUseCases.company: Streaming and Incremental ETL Pipelines (e.g., Spark, dbt)
industryUseCases.problem: Combining a historical base table with newly arrived incremental deltas during a load.
industryUseCases.solution: UNION ALL the base SELECT with the delta SELECT, then apply downstream merge/dedup logic only where keys may overlap.
industryUseCases.benefits: Cheap concatenation of base and delta, keeping all candidate rows for subsequent deterministic merge resolution.

productionDeepDive.scalability: UNION ALL parallelizes naturally: each branch can be scanned by separate workers and the results streamed together without a global synchronization barrier, making it the backbone of partition-pruned and sharded query patterns at petabyte scale.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Independent branches localize failures. In recomputable pipelines, a single failed partition scan can be retried without invalidating the others, and the deterministic concatenation makes recovery state easy to reason about.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: In federated query layers, branches may target replicas across availability zones; UNION ALL tolerates per-branch latency variance better than UNION because it does not need all rows materialized before a deduplication step.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because the output is the simple sum of inputs, rebuilding combined datasets after a restore is straightforward and verifiable by row-count reconciliation against restored sources.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Avoid an outer DISTINCT or ORDER BY unless required; push filters into each branch so partition pruning and predicate pushdown reduce scanned data before concatenation. Ensure each branch is independently optimized.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: In pay-per-byte/compute warehouses, replacing UNION with UNION ALL where deduplication is unnecessary removes sort and hash-aggregate work, directly lowering slot or credit consumption.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Each branch independently honors the access policies of its source table; UNION ALL cannot be used to bypass row-level security or column masking applied to underlying objects.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Instrument per-branch row counts and combined output count; a mismatch versus expected sums flags a dropped branch, schema drift, or an unintended switch to UNION.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use row-count reconciliation (sum of branch counts equals output count) as a cheap invariant. When deduplication is expected downstream, validate key uniqueness explicitly rather than relying on UNION ALL.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log the chosen operator and branch counts in pipeline metadata; alert when an output count is unexpectedly lower than the input sum, which can indicate someone changed UNION ALL to UNION.

recommendedPractices: **Default to UNION ALL:** Use UNION ALL unless you specifically need duplicate elimination, to avoid the hidden cost of an implicit DISTINCT.
**Align Columns Explicitly:** List columns by name in the same order in every branch rather than using SELECT *, to prevent positional mismatches.
**Tag Branch Sources:** Add a literal column identifying each branch's origin for traceability and debugging.
**Reconcile Counts:** Validate that the combined row count equals the sum of branch counts as a data-quality check.
engineeringStandards: All branches must return identical column lists in the same order with compatible data types.
ORDER BY must appear only once, after the final branch, and is understood to sort the entire result.
Choose UNION ALL over UNION deliberately and document why duplicates are or are not possible.
designRecommendations: Keep branches disjoint by design (partition by time, shard, or region) so UNION ALL is both correct and cheap.
Where overlap is possible, apply targeted deduplication (DISTINCT or windowed dedup) only on the overlapping subset, not the whole result.
Materialize the combined result as a view or table when it is queried repeatedly and inputs change infrequently.
namingConventions: Name a combining view with a clear plural or _all suffix (e.g., sales_all, orders_combined).
Use a consistent source-tag column name such as source_table or channel across all branches.
documentationStandards: Document the disjointness assumption that justifies UNION ALL over UNION.
List the source objects each branch reads and the expected total row count formula.
Note any type coercion that occurs between branches so consumers understand precision changes.
testingStrategies: Unit test that combined row count equals the sum of branch counts on representative data.
Test schema-drift detection by altering a branch column and confirming the query fails fast.
Compare UNION ALL and UNION outputs on known-overlapping fixtures to assert the expected duplicate behavior.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using UNION when UNION ALL is intended, adding a needless deduplication step.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers type UNION by habit or assume it is the safe default without realizing it performs an implicit DISTINCT.
commonMistakes.impact: Large queries run slower and cost more due to an unnecessary sort/hash; in some cases legitimately duplicate rows are silently dropped.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Default to UNION ALL and only use UNION when you have confirmed that duplicate rows must be removed.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Branches are written at different times or copied and edited, and columns are matched by position not name.
commonMistakes.impact: Values land in the wrong output columns; if the types happen to align, the query compiles and returns silently incorrect data.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Explicitly list columns in the same order in every branch and avoid SELECT * in set operations.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing ORDER BY inside an individual branch.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers expect per-branch sorting, treating each SELECT as standalone.
commonMistakes.impact: A syntax error in most dialects, or the sort is ignored, because ORDER BY applies only to the final combined result.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Put a single ORDER BY after the last branch; to control ordering across branches, add a sort-key or source-tag column.

comparisonSection.explanation: UNION ALL keeps every row including duplicates (bag semantics), while UNION removes duplicate rows via an implicit DISTINCT (set semantics). They differ in output whenever branches overlap or contain internal duplicates.

UNION ALL simply concatenates with no extra operator, so it is faster and cheaper. UNION must sort or hash the combined rows to deduplicate, adding CPU, memory, and possible disk-spill overhead on large inputs.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
beginnerQuestions.answer: UNION combines result sets and removes duplicate rows by applying an implicit DISTINCT, whereas UNION ALL combines result sets and keeps all rows including duplicates. UNION ALL is faster because it skips the deduplication step.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: State the semantic difference first (duplicates), then the performance consequence. Mention that UNION needs a sort or hash to deduplicate.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the requirements for two queries to be combined with UNION ALL?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Each query must return the same number of columns, and the columns must be in the same position with compatible (implicitly convertible) data types. Column names come from the first query.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize positional matching and type compatibility, and that names are taken from the first branch.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you prefer UNION ALL over UNION in a data pipeline?
intermediateQuestions.answer: When the branches are known to be disjoint (such as separate time partitions or shards) or when duplicate rows are meaningful and should be kept. UNION ALL avoids the costly deduplication sort/hash, lowering compute and improving scalability.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie the choice to disjointness and performance. Give the partition/shard merge as the canonical example.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is UNION ALL often faster than UNION on large datasets?
intermediateQuestions.answer: UNION must materialize and compare rows to eliminate duplicates, requiring a sort or hash aggregate that consumes CPU and memory and may spill to disk. UNION ALL just concatenates branch outputs with no comparison, so it streams and parallelizes well.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Reference the extra deduplication operator in the execution plan as the concrete reason.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does ORDER BY interact with UNION ALL?
intermediateQuestions.answer: ORDER BY may appear only once, after the final branch, and it sorts the entire combined result set rather than any individual branch. To order within branches you must add a sort-key column.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Clarify scope: ORDER BY is a property of the whole set operation, not of each SELECT.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you remove duplicates that arise only from an overlapping backfill branch without paying to deduplicate the whole result?
advancedQuestions.answer: Rather than wrapping the entire UNION ALL in DISTINCT, isolate the overlapping subset: deduplicate the backfill against the base using an anti-join or NOT EXISTS so only truly new rows are appended, then UNION ALL the cleaned delta with the base. This confines the expensive comparison to the small overlapping set.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show awareness that blanket DISTINCT is wasteful and that targeted anti-join dedup is cheaper and more correct.

advancedQuestions.question: In a sharded system, how do you guarantee correct aggregate totals when combining shards with UNION ALL?
advancedQuestions.answer: UNION ALL is correct for totals only if shards are mutually exclusive by key. You design the shard key so no row exists in two shards, then SUM/COUNT over the combined result. If a row could be replicated across shards, you must deduplicate by key (e.g., window dedup) before aggregating to avoid double counting.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The key insight is the disjointness invariant; without it, UNION ALL double-counts.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You have 24 monthly tables and need a single fast query returning all rows for the year for a dashboard. Some teammates wrote it with UNION and it is slow. What do you change and why?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Determine whether the monthly tables can contain duplicate rows across months. Since each row belongs to exactly one month, the partitions are disjoint, so deduplication is unnecessary. The slowness comes from UNION's implicit DISTINCT over millions of rows.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Replace UNION with UNION ALL across all 24 monthly SELECTs. Because months are disjoint there are no cross-branch duplicates, so the result is identical but skips the costly sort/hash, dramatically speeding the dashboard query and lowering cost.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a federated reporting layer that aggregates daily metrics from 50 regional databases into one report.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Run the same parameterized SELECT against each regional database and combine the 50 results with UNION ALL in a federation/aggregation layer, tagging each branch with its region. Regions are disjoint by design, so no deduplication is needed before SUM/COUNT.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: UNION ALL gives linear scalability and low cost but relies on the disjointness invariant; if a metric could be reported by two regions, totals would be inflated, requiring key-based dedup. Branch latency variance is tolerated because no global dedup barrier exists.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Parallelize branch execution across workers, push filters and pre-aggregation into each regional query to reduce transferred rows, and materialize the combined daily result for repeated dashboard reads. Reconcile output count against the sum of regional counts as a quality gate.

followUpQuestions: What happens to NULLs during UNION deduplication compared to UNION ALL?
Can you UNION ALL queries with different column names?
How do you sort the output of a UNION ALL by a column that exists in all branches?
What is the result type when one branch returns INT and another returns DECIMAL?
How would you detect that someone accidentally changed UNION ALL to UNION in production?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: UNION ALL concatenates the rows of two or more union-compatible SELECT queries without removing duplicates, making it faster than UNION.
keyConcepts: Bag semantics: keeps all duplicate rows.
No deduplication: skips the sort/hash that UNION requires.
Positional column matching with compatible types.
Output column names come from the first branch.
ORDER BY applies once, to the entire combined result.
formulas: Output row count = sum of each branch's row count
commands: SELECT a, b FROM t1 UNION ALL SELECT a, b FROM t2;
SELECT 'src1' AS source, a, b FROM t1 UNION ALL SELECT 'src2', a, b FROM t2 ORDER BY source, a;
SELECT * FROM base UNION ALL SELECT * FROM delta WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM base b WHERE b.id = delta.id);
interviewPoints: UNION ALL keeps duplicates; UNION removes them.
UNION ALL is faster: no dedup sort/hash.
Columns matched by position, not name.
Default to UNION ALL; escalate to UNION only when dedup is required.
Correct totals require disjoint branches (no cross-branch duplicates).
quickNotes: Every branch must return the same number of columns with compatible types.
Names and aliases are taken from the first SELECT only.
ORDER BY goes after the final branch and sorts the whole result.
For overlapping backfills, dedup the overlap with an anti-join rather than DISTINCT on everything.
Reconcile output count = sum of branch counts to catch dropped branches or accidental UNION.

keyTakeaways: UNION ALL concatenates result sets and keeps all rows including duplicates, using bag semantics, whereas UNION removes duplicates with an implicit DISTINCT.
Because it skips the deduplication sort/hash, UNION ALL is significantly faster and cheaper, making it the default primitive for merging disjoint partitions and shards.
Branches are matched by column position with compatible types, and output names come from the first SELECT, so explicit aligned column lists prevent silent errors.
UNION ALL only yields correct totals when branches are disjoint; if overlap is possible, deduplicate the overlapping subset with an anti-join instead of a blanket DISTINCT.
Reconciling the combined row count against the sum of branch counts is a cheap, powerful invariant for detecting dropped branches or an accidental switch to UNION.
